en: Now begins the fifth supplement: the narrative of the slaying of Kaṃsa.
[1] Now, in the assembly hall of the illustrious King of Vraja, which was illuminated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there was again a morning discourse, as follows:
[2] Snigdhakaṇṭha said:
Then night arrived;
and when it had dawned, Śivā, who was becoming highly auspicious, became propitious toward Śrī-Kṛṣṇa.

While it was clear that [the night] would be inauspicious for Kaṃsa, and as that night— which gave birth to great terror for him in both sleep and wakefulness— passed away, that deceitful man again prepared for the commencement of the profound wrestling match. Then the arena floor, situated in the center of a vast array of bright platforms belonging to those who were adorned and those who were not, shone with its radiant and variegated decorations.
Like a star-studded sky above autumn clouds flashing with lightning, Kaṃsa himself occupied the highest throne there, acting as the crest-jewel of all wicked kings;
yet, though this was possible due to his being seized by the pride of sovereignty, it resulted only in his own state of terror. And therein—
That which Akrūra and Ānakadundubhi performed on their own bed at its two ends—
placing the daughter of Devaka among the crowds of citizens while Nanda and others were far away—
and furthermore, that he stationed the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa at the gate upon the tip of his own trunk; [all this was done by the Lord].
Since that Bhoja king treated the Mallas with deceit, who would not be provoked by him?
Furthermore, there—
whatever musical instruments were played at the command of Kaṃsa, appropriate for the occasion of the wrestling match—

That very thing became an auspicious omen for the departure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. (2) Then, when the two of them entered the vicinity of the gates of Raṅgapura after having performed their morning rites— while the group of elder cowherds had been sent ahead by them themselves, who did not come in person, in order to manifest their own unimpeded power— [the following occurred].
At that time, however, everyone perceived everything solely from the clamor of the world.
Then, wishing to determine whether it was a mountain or an elephant— [the elephant] being ever-fierce, fierce with rut, and with temporal juice trickling down—
he, putting on his garment and tightening his head-ornament to crush the shameless Kuvalayāpīḍa, was followed by a multitude of friends of his elder brother.
The crusher of enemies took the lead himself;
and when his own friends there tried to restrain him with words, as did his enemies, the monkey looked upon both with a mere smile and entered the elephant. (Anuṣṭubh)

[6] And then, by the glorious Hari, there was the seeking of that path; the propitiation even of that enraged elephant; the repeated turning of his own body toward the marks of its trunk and tusks; and the liberation from it thereafter.
Pulling at its tail, whirling it about, facing it and striking it, fleeing from it and suddenly falling upon it, rushing after its heavy charge and causing it to whirl in confusion; then,
when its tusks have been evaded, agitating it by striking the ground and turning away— again and again.
By the maneuver of drawing near and seizing him by the forelock, he caused him to fall upon the surface of the earth;
then, mounting his body and snapping his various limbs with his teeth, he slew him.
To the onlookers, this led to a rising and sinking like the waves of the ocean. (Sragdharā metre)

When the elephant has been killed, talk of its keepers is useless; but when the wrestler is crushed, what then can be said of the lice residing upon him? (2.5.6) [7] And at that time, this is the distinction:
Wandering about, he was indeed a dancer; destroying, he was indeed a lion;
and breaking, he was indeed a thunderbolt—thus was Hari perceived by the elephant.
Having slain the serpent and seized its pair of tusks...
The enemy of Kaṃsa gave one of them to his brother, as if thinking: "May that fame which is produced by the two of us be destined to abide in both of us equally on all sides. (Śālinī meter)
The lion killed the elephant; there, Bala too was covered with drops of blood and rut,
standing by its side as an attendant.
Just as if by a shadow, he then wandered about.
( Rathoddhatā ) [8] Thus, even the gods, fearing the roar of his thundering voice, became known by the name Asvapnas ("Sleepless") because they never slept;

and this elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, though preeminent in the flow of his rut-fluid, received a gift made with that very rut-fluid— whereupon those scribes, out of wonder, were as if themselves mere lines of writing.
And that being so, no one out of fear suddenly spoke to Kaṃsa;
and thereafter—
those rays of light, beautified by the royal garments plundered in the forenoon.
With their hands holding the tusks of a great elephant just slaughtered,
and with armlets and bracelets fashioned from its blood, the two of them entered before the king with such elephants. (Vasantatilakā)
Valor alone is the ornament of a man, wherein even that which is to be discarded becomes worthy of praise;
for the drops of blood and rut from the elephants stain his body.
In the assembly of Kaṃsa, those two did not shine.
Then his enemies beheld Bhīṣma’s body, unconquered, standing before them; while those with hearts full of affection saw him as one standing in the midst, the very embodiment of peace.

There too, they clearly perceived its manifold distinctions; just as the state of being [is perceived], so this [state] manifests intensely and simultaneously. (Śikhariṇī) Or rather, how much could be described here of its excellence of sweetness?

Now, let even a small portion of that splendor be described, which was saluted by hundreds of thousands of people in the assembly while Kaṃsa was still alive— a splendor before which the Bhoja king, though breathing, was regarded by the gods as if dead.

(Mandākrāntā meter) [10] Then, having arrived with lotus stalks held in their hands like elephants with tusks, those two of broad chests and praiseworthy deeds looked at Kaṃsa with disdainful glances and touched him on the back, asking, "Is this indeed he?"
Then, casting their glances here and there, they both looked about;
and turning back, the glorious Hari saw once more that he was following along the very path of heaven.
"Therefore, his departure from there must not be too far away," he said, laughing; and having rejoiced with all his friends, he related to one another the wonderful events that had occurred.

[12] Then, upon merely beholding his body— which, being reddened by the blood of the elephant he himself had slain, appeared like the vessel of the world at the time of universal dissolution, manifesting a dark-blue and crimson hue—
Kaṃsa’s splendor was destroyed; as he cried out, "Who are these two?", those standing nearby said to him,
"These very ones are they."
Kaṃsa said:
"What is seen on these two hands? Or by whom has the body been made into a vessel for painting?"
[14] They all said,
"The two tusks of Kuvalayāpīḍa appear to be severed, and his body must have become stained red with its blood.
[15] Kaṃsa, with feigned indignation and agitation, said, "Ho there!"
"Enveloped in distress, both of these are impossible, serving as nothing more than mere words.
Then, since they had offered no reply and were overcome by fear, he himself made their power known to them. For it was said:
"O Kaṃsa, if you yourself are powerful, then shame on that [other power]!"

"Why do you perceive the elephant at the gate, yet not your own body there? If you say he is superior because of his two tusks, then why do you not seize those two [tusks] as we have seized [you]?"—this is what was suggested by that person through their own gesture. (Śikhariṇī meter)
[17] This being the case— this very same [Lord] slew Pūtanā, overturned the cart, crushed that Daitya Marut, and likewise crushed the two Arjunas, and so forth.
O people! While he was formerly watching the divine pastimes of Gokula, you tormented those [demons];
and even now, while he watches, you continue to torment them. Behold others [who are being tormented] as they listen!
And there, by the expansion of his eyes, he seeks to drink in the entirety of their forms simultaneously with those two eyes.

As if to lick all sweetness with the movement of the tongue of her description, her nostrils were clearly flared out of pride at the occasion of its attainment; as if to draw all fragrance within herself, she repeatedly pressed those two hands against them; and as if to embrace every limb along with the whole body, she embraced him.

While he was seeking happiness and desiring truth amidst the creation of gods and men, and while the various musical instruments resounded, a hymn of praise granting all happiness issued from the mouths of everyone.
This very excellence of his power manifested, constantly overwhelming all other meditations.
In that situation, even though the wrestlers had been previously incited by Kaṃsa to speak disparagingly for the sake of battle, they ended up offering praise instead.
For instance, this being the case, the one named Cāṇūra, whose nature was cruel, spoke thus: "O son of Nanda! [20] Thus it stands.

The two forms of address, "O Rāma" (using his father’s name) and [the other] without that name, were set in motion by Sarasvatī for the purpose of conveying a different understanding; yet, for the sake of praise,
her organ of speech was made to dance as if they were identical,
since both boys were equal incarnations— one through the name of his father and the other through his own name— possessing excellent conduct and noble behavior.
"Listen," Śrī Kṛṣṇa said with a smile,
"let it be commanded as you wish."
[22] Cāṇūra said:
"To what extent should your good fortune be placed within my mind?
[23] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Of what kind?"
[24] Cāṇūra said:
"O Great King, these feet of yours shine forth, their very nature being the desire to behold the grace of Your Majesty.
[25] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
—“True;
let some further task for us be assigned.
Cāṇūra said:
"This which you have both agreed upon is indeed consistent;
nevertheless, your perpetual turning away from this does not bring us joy.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

"We are men who dwell in the forest; we do not follow the principles of policy or conduct practiced by those counted among the royal assembly. However, now following your instruction alone, we shall act in accordance with the customs of this country.
Cāṇūra said:
"Now, whatever the feet of the best of kings command regarding you two,
let that be carried out again.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke thus, as if with humility.
"O preeminent wrestler,
please give your command as you see fit.
Cāṇūra replied:
"Then, may you two enjoy the pleasure of play here together with us.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said,
"Our playful glances toward children are indeed pleasing even to kings."
But you instead resort to mere lamentation;
therefore, this exposure to ridicule belongs to you alone, and it is not fitting for your majesties who possess royal splendor.
Cāṇūra said: "I swear by the feet of the king;
this is indeed the command of the kings."
[33] Śrī-Kṛṣṇa said: "How so?
[34] Cāṇūra said:
"You are but a child; you have not yet crushed Pūtanā and the others, nor have you displayed such prowess."

"O Youth, you are not yet fit for this task, being occupied with the various sports of supporting the mountains!"— from these words of the King, who was like a young elephant whose labor of subduing the world-elephants was directly witnessed, there arose great wonder. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)
[35] But this one of yours is superior; he is indeed superior by virtue of the act of slaughtering Pralamba and the others.
[36] Śrī-Kṛṣṇa said:
"Due solely to the sin of their vain hatred toward us, those others met with such a transformation."

And Mount Parvata himself became such [a mountain] by his own accord, having acquired the status of a "mountain of sacrifices" (makha-parvata) for the purpose of humbling the pride of the thousand-armed one (Rāvaṇa).

As for us, however, we conduct ourselves entirely and in every way exactly as we are. Furthermore, our bow—having been worn out by antiquity as if infested with woodworms in the past—became cracked of its own accord due to being scattered from afar; thus, upon merely being touched, it fell apart.

And Kuvalayāpīḍa, rushing forward to crush me as I was retreating, suddenly found himself unable to withdraw his two tusks once they had plunged deep into the earth; yet, by the very act of striking, he broke them even as they were snapping, thereby destroying his own life.
In various places, I was perceived by the people—who were seized by the scent of my speed—as the very cause of that event.
Likewise, the elephant-keepers who were beneath him perished only after the elephant had fallen;
do not think otherwise.
Cāṇūra said:
This which you say, with a shrinking mind, is entirely improper;
for great-minded kings do not harbor lingering resentment in such matters, but rather, they dispatched them there specifically to humble the pride of the arrogant who had long resided by their side.
Because of the reversal of those who have spent their special efforts in vain, they desire that you two alone shall provide for their own strength.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"That is a source of great wonder and good fortune for us."
However, we feel ashamed to praise ourselves by our own praise, thinking,
"We shall perform service even to attain the rank of Indra for this illustrious Great King.
Nevertheless, our hearts shrink back, thinking, "We have not mastered the science of wrestling."
Cāṇūra said:
"Do not vainly deny even this,
which has been heard and is well known."
Indeed, while the cowherds are engaged in tending the cattle, they are constantly practicing our science.
Therefore, with sincerity, both we and you must obey the commands of the kings; they are not to be transgressed.
[40] Śrī-Kṛṣṇa said:
"Nevertheless, since that auspicious knowledge does not exist among us forest-dwellers, we shall immediately adopt your instruction and proceed ourselves to cause the king’s death.
[41] Then, having extended this news as far as the two tusks of an elephant, they struck Kaṃsa’s chest as if with those very tusks.

Quickly suspecting him, he buried his fist; then, struck by Cāṇūra’s fist-blow which left his arm hanging limp, he was ensnared by Cāṇūra—who, like the younger brother of the bird [Garuḍa] who rides upon him, had gained renown for his strength and was like a divine lion playing with a great elephant due to his novelty. And there, as they displayed their prowess hand-to-hand, arm-to-arm, and foot-to-foot, a great struggle ensued.
With the clashing of knees and the striking of hips against hips, their anger was fully aroused;
as they fought fist-to-fist and palm-to-palm, how could one possibly conceive of the many varieties of that battle between Hari and the wrestler? (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)

But Kṛṣṇa and Kāmapāla held Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika by the hands, and while Kaṃsa was obstructed from breathing, they brought about his obstruction of life. Therein, one thing occurred that was wondrous, as it were, being far beyond the reach of all knowledge.

When Hari drew back his own limb with its constituent parts, and when he placed it [on the opponent], then a powerful reversal manifested in the wrestler; moreover, even from afar, the method of striking and so forth repeatedly found its counterpart. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)

Even as the two wrestlers struck Madhava and Rama with truth, those two, swelling with speed, did not even reach that mark. (Anuṣṭubh) [42] This being the case, for those who had not experienced His power and even for those who had, there was only the proclamation of faults directed against Kaṃsa.

In that regard, concerning the Mallas of the East as well: first of all, this was their reflection— “These two may indeed be very young and very strong, but they do not know the most excellent science of wrestling.”
Therefore, for what reason does the king employ us— who have reached the further shore of those very sciences— in this conflict? (Śālinī meter) [43] But at the end—

Even a coward employed this in battle.
(Śālinī meter) [44] Likewise, others who were abounding in women and devoid of cruelty reported the faults to Kaṃsa, saying:
"Where are the wrestlers with bodies like adamantine mountains, and where are those two exceedingly delicate ones?"
These two are but children; therefore, fie upon those who consent to this and fie upon the sovereigns!
How could they not be censurable, we who, though in this assembly that hates the virtuous, cast our gaze upon them as if with curiosity? (Śikhariṇī)
Fie upon our merit, for despite even a mere fraction of Hari’s glance, this calamity—
resembling a demon to the community of His devotees— has arisen;
such that one who was traveling to Vraja in the morning returns to Vraja itself in the evening.

"Those women for whom happiness flows—these supreme ones of excellent merit! (Śikhariṇī meter) Fie on us, who have followed after Kaṃsa out of fear; how many of those women with the eyes of the best of Vraja do we praise, who are indeed capable of uttering the name of Hari?"

Those who always sing of his virtues, even while engaged in many tasks at their own homes, and who constantly dwell upon them in their hearts at every step—for whom is this incomparable fruit? That his very form [is thus honored]. (Śikhariṇī meter)
The peerless essence of loveliness, spontaneously perfected,
the absolute abode of both splendor and fame, these [eyes] always drink it with their glances from every side, appearing ever-new in its radiance.
(In the Vasantatilakā meter:
Who is able to describe the supreme greatness of their love? Behold, having abandoned everything else, our minds have followed after them.
Since Govinda attracts the hearts of all— even those who are merely his followers— by means of his splendor consisting of spiritual labor, he is rightly named Saṅkarṣaṇa.

(Mandākrāntā meter) Even while charging toward his enraged enemy, Hari shines forth, displaying his own gentleness without abandoning it, as he bears drops of sweat from the thrill of passion upon his lotus-like face with a smiling expression.
That Rāma’s face and eyes are clearly red shines forth from his anger;
yet that too is his natural state, for he is the very fire of Hari’s majesty in person.
These [persons] are surrounded by Śrī Vasudeva and Nanda, and joined by Śrī Devakī.

Since all virtuous people, upon hearing my words which possess an inner flame of fire, repeatedly become agitated while casting a piercing gaze upon Kaṃsa, his destruction alone will be accomplished without delay. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)
[45] Then, as they experienced that power, there arose a proclamation of Kaṃsa’s faults,
as follows: "This fool, who out of fear placed the wrestlers within himself before the presence of Murāri..."
Just as a certain hunter, concealing his own identity, sets village lions before a lion;
he who brought about the destruction of the power of Pūtanā and the other demons.
He who humbled even the pride of Śakra, and who deluded every creator except for the one devoid of reasoning— him,
it is said, the King of the Bhojas overcomes and indeed rules over completely.
(Vasantatilaka) Where is Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is self-luminous, and where is the host of wrestlers, who are characterized by darkness?
Behold the wondrous battle between these two, like that between light and shadow! (Anuṣṭubh)
Even in their mutual struggle, no contact is seen between Kṛṣṇa and the wrestler,
due to the excellence of the former's power, like that between light and darkness.
(Anuṣṭubh) Even swelling or bloodshed is not observed on the body of the adversary.
Not even a trace of arrogance arises in the Enemy of the Daityas;
behold, as he faces his foes, his preeminent valor, appearing like poison,
repeatedly shatters the entire vital core of each enemy into powder.

A subtle fire [destroys] a mass of grass, lightning a mountain, the fire born from the friction of wood-sticks the ocean, the sun the darkness, and likewise even the name of the Enemy of Mura destroys every sin.

In the same way, let this victorious son of Nanda be beheld from within the arena by the wrestlers, who are bristling with a multitude of powerful and massive bodies. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter) Here, let the supreme wonder of Kṛṣṇa in battle be witnessed.
Cāṇūra was crushed by him, and Kaṃsa’s throat was split. (2.5.36) Nevertheless, that fool struck Hari with his diamond-hard fists;
with those two [fists] lodged in his chest, he experienced horripilation out of genuine pride. (2.5.37)
[46] Thus, while surveying the world with its lamentations and its celestial beings, Hari too, laughing once and gazing at him as he whirled through the sky, seized him.
He said, "Shame on you, you are dead! and with intense contempt, he dashed him to the ground even as the king looked on;
and he, having gained satisfaction by that fist which had been rendered useless by his own fist—*Rucirā*.
The blow of Bala’s palm, which resulted in the destruction of his life— [that blow] which,
at first, with its violent force, shook the entire mass of his limbs on all sides; and which,
by its fierce appearance, repeatedly caused his pair of eyes to roll about, agitating them.
Crushed by the dark-hued Name of Rāma, that wrestler, who had swiftly pointed out the path for Kaṃsa, went quickly to another world; it is a marvel that he was seen everywhere in every direction.

(Śārdūlavikrīḍita) Then, having played with those two, and having recognized the strength of the crusher of Baka there—not [excessive]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

When those two experts showered the surface of the earth with contemptuous glances, then there arrived the one named Kūṭa and the one from Tośala joined by Śala; having instantly crushed each of them with blows from their left feet and hands, they performed a dance. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)

[47] Then, another group of Mallas, though equal in number, also considered it necessary to form a collective force against that very assembly. [48] But when those Mallas had been slain, other Śṛgālas arrived;
while Kṛṣṇa and Rāma were looking on, they made the leaders laugh. (Anuṣṭubh)

O King, just as I previously dispatched commanders of your army even to the third heaven to conquer [the enemy], so too have I today dispatched an elephant for your sake and arranged wrestlers for that purpose.
Thus, by providing you with comfort on that path, I rejoice along with my own friends.
"Let him play," Kaṃsa reportedly directed in the assembly; there Kṛṣṇa indeed played.

(Sragdharā) In the midst of the games between the two brothers and their friends, there were frequent defeats; having struck them down, he repeatedly transferred his own inner state into Kaṃsa’s heart. (Anuṣṭubh)

[49] Thus, being treated with wonder by Maitreyikā and praised by the four castes, equal in honor, honoring their peers of the same age, named Rāma and Rāmānuja, resplendent from the joy of having mastered the irreproachable musical sciences of heaven and earth, they attained the rhythmic measures of the *malla* dance by virtue of rivaling divine dancing.

Having gathered celestial chariots from all directions for that festival, and having been honored by the virtuous with their flowers, the two of them fashioned all those who were devoted to the single path into a single hour.
Unable to endure this, Kaṃsa, perceiving the identity between wealth and power as if they were synonymous, [acted].

Because his own speech—characterized by such things as the seizing of the cowherds' wealth, which was to be described later—was observed to be failing two or three times on his left hand, he prohibited his own musical instrument. When that musical instrument of Siddheśvara had been thus prohibited, it became established in its purity; and when it was established, it became beneficial through its radiance.

Accompanied by his circle of friends, he heard those various harsh words addressed to Vasudeva, the lord of Vraja, as well as to Ugrasena; having suddenly perceived both of these as targets for the affliction of his own vulnerability, the independent enemy of Kaṃsa, possessing a thousand faces, leaped up with great force.
Therefore, he suddenly gazed upon the very platform where Kaṃsa stood;

there, the unbearable splendor of Śrī Hari’s form had assumed a physical combat with him. Then Kaṃsa, his destruction having arrived, his mind defeated by that vanquisher of himself, abandoned his fortitude and moved about, grasping sword and shield.
How did he, who was so difficult to overcome and possessed of a joyful gait—that very one who is the refuge of the Vraja clan—come to have his hair seized and be driven away?
Indeed, even he, having entered the lineage of the Moon (Śaśada), was unable to endure it, like a hare unable to endure a lion.
And the world sang this in verse: [53] The world, however, expressed this in a verse:—

Like a hawk seizing a pigeon, like a five-faced lion seizing a lordly elephant, or like the thunderbolt shattering a mountain, may he who roars fiercely, having suddenly seized Kaṃsa and brought him under his control, be victorious.
He performs his play all around, moving in a wide arc.
(Vasantatilakā) [54] Thus, when the world had been made famous by Hari, that Lord of the Bhojas, having his hair seized, first surrendered half of his life;

then, as he was falling headlong from the couch because he had been snorted at, he surrendered the other half. Even Hari was unable to perceive the speed of that act, due to being overcome by the desire to fight.
Kaṃsa’s hair was seized by Hari, and his life-breaths passed into Hari’s fist;
yet this is not surprising— remember his childhood.
And that [act] of drawing away the breast-milk of Pūtanā.
With sword and shield falling, jeweled armor slipping away, all his hair disheveled and his head-dress tumbling down; (Indravajrā meter).
That utterly deluded man, having climbed upon it, fell down from the bed in front of the people below.
(bhujaṅga-prayātā) Previously his eyelashes were motionless, and as he was struck with fear, so too did Kaṃsa perish; thus,
because he had met his death through him, no one among the cowards spoke out.
